description.value: The study examined neuronal responses to visual food cues in obesity-resistant and obesity-prone adults in fasted and acute fed states.

spans.text: The objective of this study was to examine the differences in neuronal response to visual food cues in adults recruited as either obesity-resistant (OR) or obesity-prone (OP)

value: We hypothesized that an acute meal would result in significantly greater attenuation of the neuronal response to visual food cues ... in OR as compared to OP individuals.

spans.text: We hypothesized that an acute meal would result in significantly greater attenuation of the neuronal response to visual food cues (in a network of brain regions including the insula and prefrontal cortex) in OR as compared to OP individuals.

In the fed state, obesity-prone individuals showed greater activation in medial and anterior prefrontal cortex than obesity-resistant individuals, while obesity-resistant individuals showed greater attenuation of insula, inferior prefrontal cortex, and medial prefrontal cortex response. These findings suggest that the neuronal response to food cues is altered in individuals prone to weight gain and obesity and may represent a core feature of obesity risk rather than a consequence of increased fat mass.
